title: Pre-Purchase Inspection Fujairah | Tankers at Anchorage
description: Pre-purchase ship inspection at Fujairah anchorage and berths: tankers, bunker barges and bulk carriers checked on deck, in tanks and machinery for the buyer.
h1: Inspecting a second-hand tanker for a buyer while she waits off Fujairah
intro: Many tankers that change hands are seen by their buyers at Fujairah, because the ship is already stopped there for bunkers, orders or a ship-to-ship transfer. That stop is the inspection window, and it can close as soon as a charterer's orders arrive. Our pre-purchase inspection at Fujairah measures as well as looks: deck and ballast tank structure, spot thickness readings, crack checks at known fatigue details and running readings on whatever machinery the chief engineer can operate. We cover crude and product tankers at anchor, bunker barges at their lay-by berths and bulk carriers before they load. The team flies in from India and reaches the ship by launch.

highlights.h: Built for a ship that may sail
highlights.p: At Fujairah the buyer rarely controls the timetable. Before boarding we agree a ranked list of spaces with the buyer's superintendent, so ballast tanks, deck and pump room are covered first, and whatever has been seen is reported to the buyer before the launch takes the team ashore.

highlights.h: Gulf heat shows in the steel
highlights.p: Tankers that have spent years trading in and out of the Gulf carry the marks of hot decks and warm, saline ballast water. We look hardest at cargo-tank deckheads, deck longitudinals and ballast tank coatings, where those conditions bring wastage forward of the class timetable.

A tanker coming off a storage contract may have lain at anchor for months with her main engine stopped. The inspection looks for what long idleness leaves behind: neglected auxiliaries, deferred maintenance, and sea chests and strainers in whatever state the engineers find them when they open up.

sections.h: Where can a ship be inspected for a buyer at Fujairah?
p: Most viewings happen at the anchorage. A tanker waiting for bunkers, a berth or a charterer's orders is boarded from a launch booked through the seller's agent, with the team carrying portable ultrasonic gauges, a magnetic particle kit, vibration and thermal instruments and its own gas monitors. At anchor the buyer sees the deck, the accommodation, the engine room, the pump room and any ballast tank the crew has emptied, ventilated and certified safe. The shell below the waterline cannot be seen there, so its condition is judged from the last docking report and the class records.

Alongside berths give a different set of opportunities. Bulk carriers loading aggregates at the port's bulk berths can be inspected on arrival, when the holds are still empty and dry. Bunker barges and small coastal tankers are best seen at their lay-by berths between supply runs, when the operator can spare them for a day. An idle tanker at an oil terminal berth in the Fujairah Oil Industry Zone may allow deck and pump-room work if the terminal issues a permit, but cargo-tank entry there is unusual.
list: Anchorage, by launch: crude and product tankers waiting for bunkers, orders, a berth or a ship-to-ship transfer
Floating storage tankers at anchor: longer stays on board, but cargo tanks usually full
Bulk and general cargo berths: holds and hatch covers on bulk carriers before aggregate loading starts
Bunker barge lay-by berths: end-to-end inspection of barges and coastal tankers between supply runs
Oil terminal berths: deck, piping and pump room only, under the terminal's permit

sections.h: Which ships change hands at Fujairah, and what should a buyer check?
p: Product tankers in the MR and LR sizes, Aframaxes, Suezmaxes and VLCCs make up most of the work, because Fujairah sits on the route every Gulf tanker takes and many sales are agreed while a ship is between voyages. Older crude tankers are often bought for further trading in regional and storage roles, and their buyers need to know how much life is left in the ballast tanks and the deck before the next renewal survey. Bunker barges and coastal tankers serving the anchorage pass between regional operators; they work hard, come alongside other ships many times a day and age quickly around the fendering and the side shell.

Bulk carriers that call to load rock and aggregates from the emirate's quarries are the main dry cargo candidates. A Handysize or Supramax in that trade has abrasive cargo on its tank top and lower hold frames, and grab and loader contact on the hopper plating, so those are the areas a buyer's inspection concentrates on, together with the hatch covers and cranes that load and protect the cargo.

sections.h: How is a pre-purchase inspection scoped for a tanker at Fujairah anchorage?
p: The scope starts from what the crew can make safe. Cargo tanks on a trading tanker are rarely gas-free at anchor, so the buyer's evidence on cargo-tank structure comes from the deck, the class records and the last thickness report. Ballast tanks are the priority for entry: double-bottom and double-side spaces on a double-hull tanker, the forepeak and the aft peak. We ask the buyer to request, through the broker, that the seller empties and ventilates the agreed tanks before the team boards, because preparing a tank at anchor takes hours the window may not have.

Deck plating over the cargo tanks is read on a grid, because a thickness reading taken from above also shows steel lost from the underside, which is where inert gas and condensation attack the deckhead. Deck longitudinals cannot be reached from above, so their condition waits for an adjoining ballast space or a record. The pump room is entered under the ship's permit system for pump casings, bulkhead penetrations and bilge structure. In the hot months, deck work is planned for the early morning and late afternoon, because plating in direct sun becomes too hot for standard couplant and probes, and for the technicians holding them.

Bunkering shapes the day as well. While a bunker barge is alongside, the deck crew is busy at the manifold and access around it is closed, so tank entry and deck readings move elsewhere until bunkering ends. A ship-to-ship transfer halts inspection on deck altogether, and the team works in the engine room or waits until the hoses are disconnected.

sections.h: What do pre-purchase inspections at Fujairah usually find?
p: Findings on Gulf-trading tankers and the craft that serve them follow a recognisable pattern. The list below is what buyers most often have to weigh, each item tied to the conditions that produce it, and the report sorts them into items for the seller to clear, points to raise in the negotiation and work for the new owner's first docking.
list: Pitting and general wastage on cargo-tank deckheads and deck longitudinals, read through the deck plating and seen from adjoining ballast spaces
Ballast tank coating breakdown at edges, welds and horizontal stringers, moving coatings from FAIR towards POOR and exposing steel to warm seawater
Grooving along bottom longitudinals and at bracket toes in the double bottom, where water lies after deballasting
Corroded deck piping supports, vent heads and walkways weakened by heat and spray
Dents, set-in plating and wasted shell at the fender line on bunker barges that come alongside many ships
Auxiliary machinery running rough after a long spell at anchor, picked up by vibration readings on pumps and generators
Hot spots at switchboard connections under load, more likely in engine rooms running at high ambient temperatures

sections.h: How should a buyer plan an inspection at Fujairah?
p: Tell us about Fujairah as soon as the ship is expected to call there, even if the date is approximate. UAE visas are arranged before the team flies, usually into Dubai or Sharjah with a road crossing to the east coast afterwards, so the earliest boarding date depends on how early we hear. Keep us informed of the ship's ETA: anchorage waits shorten without warning, and a ship that was expected to wait several days can be called to a berth or ordered away the morning after the team arrives.

The seller's agent books the launch and any port entry permit, and the buyer asks the seller, through the broker, for consent to the spaces on the inspection plan and for the class records to be released by the classification society. Boarding goes ahead only when the buyer, the agent and the master confirm it, and the team follows the owner's and the agent's security instructions for the Gulf of Oman in force at the time. If the visit is cut short, the report states plainly what was seen and what was not, so the buyer can ask for the rest at the next port or decide on what is known.

sections.h: Example scope: a crude tanker leaving floating storage at Fujairah
p: A buyer considering a Suezmax that has spent months as floating storage off Fujairah faces two questions at once: what state the hull is in after years in Gulf trades, and what the storage period has done to machinery that seldom ran. A typical plan gives the first part of the visit to the ballast tanks the crew has prepared, reading bottom and side shell plating, longitudinals and bracket toes in the double bottom and double sides, and rating the coatings space by space. The deck grid, the pump room, the deck piping and the mooring fittings follow.

In the engine room the chief engineer runs what can be run at anchor: generators, ballast and cooling pumps, purifiers, compressors and the fans. Vibration readings on those machines are compared with each other, and the switchboards are surveyed with a thermal camera under whatever load the ship can produce. The maintenance records for the storage period are checked against running hours, because jobs deferred while a ship sat at anchor tend to fall due together. The report then separates conditions likely to concern class, which most memoranda leave with the seller, from those the buyer would inherit.

vessels: VLCC, Suezmax and Aframax crude tankers
codes: Norwegian Saleform 2012 and SALEFORM 2025 – the buyers' right to inspect
IACS UR Z10.1 (oil tankers) and Z10.4 (double-hull oil tankers) – enhanced hull surveys
IACS UR Z7 – hull classification surveys, with the GOOD, FAIR and POOR coating terms
SOLAS XI-1/2 and the International Code on the Enhanced Programme of Inspections (2011 ESP Code)
ASTM E797 – standard practice for manual pulse-echo contact thickness measurement
ISO 20816-1 – measurement and evaluation of machine vibration
deliverables: Findings that could change the buyer's decision, reported before the team leaves the anchorage
Condition of ballast tanks, deck and pump room, with coating ratings and located photographs
Deck grid and ballast tank thickness readings against as-built or last-report values
Vibration and thermal readings on the machinery run at anchor, with its operating condition
Notes on the class records, last thickness report and any CAP report the seller releases
Spaces and items not inspected, each with the reason

faqs.q: Can a pre-purchase inspection be done at Fujairah anchorage?
faqs.a: Yes, and most are. The team boards from a launch the seller's agent books and works through the spaces the seller has agreed to open. Ballast tanks, deck, pump room, accommodation and engine room are the usual scope at anchor. Cargo tanks are rarely gas-free on a trading tanker, so their structure is judged from deck readings and the records, and the shell below the waterline is assessed from the last docking report.

faqs.q: What happens if the tanker gets orders and sails during the inspection?
faqs.a: We plan for it. The buyer's priorities are ranked before boarding, so the spaces that matter most are seen first, and the buyer hears what we have found before the team goes ashore. The report records what was covered and what was not. The buyer can then ask for the remainder at the ship's next port, or decide on what is known within the period the memorandum allows.

faqs.q: Can you inspect a tanker that has been on floating storage off Fujairah?
faqs.a: Yes. A storage stay often gives more time on board than a trading call, although the cargo tanks are usually full. We concentrate on ballast tanks, deck, pump room and machinery, and check the maintenance and running-hours records for the storage period, since deferred work tends to fall due at once. Machinery that has stood idle is run where the chief engineer can do so safely, and its vibration readings show how it is running.

faqs.q: Do you inspect bunker barges and coastal tankers for buyers at Fujairah?
faqs.a: Yes, usually at their lay-by berths between supply runs, when the operator can release them for the day. A barge is small enough to cover from end to end: tanks the crew can make safe, side shell and fendering zones, deck and piping, pumps and generators. These craft come alongside other ships many times a day, so dents, set-in plating and wasted shell at the fender line are the findings buyers weigh most.

faqs.q: Will the classification society accept readings from a Fujairah pre-purchase inspection?
faqs.a: No, and a pre-purchase inspection does not need it to. Class gives survey credit only to thickness readings taken by a firm that the ship's own society has accepted under IACS UR Z17, while Atlantis is still going through that process with DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. What we measure at Fujairah is evidence for the buyer, set beside the class records and thickness reports the seller releases through the classification society.

faqs.q: How does the inspection team reach a ship at Fujairah from India?
faqs.a: The technicians fly from India, normally into Dubai or Sharjah because those airports have more direct services than Fujairah's own, then drive across the Hajar mountains to the east coast. UAE visas are arranged before travel, so send the ship's name, expected dates and the buyer's priorities to info@atlantisndt.com as soon as Fujairah is on her itinerary. The seller's agent books the launch and port permits.
